claims.claim: Out of all investigated cortical measures, only average thickness of the PT, bilaterally, was related to participants' language experience at p=0.01.
claims.source: Out of all investigated cortical measures, only average thickness of the PT, bilaterally, was related to participants' language experience at p=0.01, see Table 2.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports statistical findings from the exploratory analysis.

claims.claim: Participants with more extensive and diverse language experience had a significantly thinner PT.
claims.source: Specifically, participants with more extensive and diverse language experience had a significantly thinner PT.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the direction of the relationship found.

claims.claim: On average, participants had 2.375 gyri in the left hemisphere (SD = 0.63), and 1.84 in the right (SD = 0.64).
claims.source: On average, participants had 2.375 gyri in the left hemisphere (SD = 0.63), and 1.84 in the right (SD = 0.64).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports descriptive statistics from the TASH segmentation.

claims.claim: The number of gyri was not related to participants' language experience, either in the left (β = 0.10, t = 0.97, p=0.335), or in the right hemisphere (β = – 0.01, t = – 0.13, p=0.90).
claims.source: The number of gyri was not related to participants' language experience, either in the left (β = 0.10, t = 0.97, p=0.335), or in the right hemisphere (β = – 0.01, t = – 0.13, p=0.90), according to a linear model with number of gyri as dependent and language experience as independent variables (controlling for participants' age and sex).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports statistical test results.

claims.claim: Only average thickness of the second TTG (bilaterally) was related to participants' language experience at p<0.01.
claims.source: Out of all investigated cortical measures, only average thickness of the second TTG (bilaterally) was related to participants' language experience at p<0.01, see Appendix 1—table 3.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports the main finding from the TTG analysis.

claims.claim: A cluster of vertices negatively related to participants' language experience at p<0.0001 (uncorrected) was found in the superior aspect of the left STG, corresponding to the location of the second TTG.
claims.source: We found one cluster of vertices negatively related to participants' language experience at p<0.0001 (uncorrected), located in the superior aspect of the left STG, corresponding to the location of the second TTG, see Appendix 1—figure 5.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports findings from the vertex-wise analysis.

claims.claim: At the same threshold, no vertices were found in the right hemisphere, possibly due to greater anatomical variability in right compared to left auditory regions.
claims.source: At the same threshold, no vertices were found in the right hemisphere, possibly due to greater, known anatomical variability in right compared to left auditory regions (Dalboni da Rocha et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports negative findings and provides a cited explanation.

claims.claim: The model containing phoneme level information explained the most variance in the average thickness of the bilateral second TTG.
claims.source: The analyses showed that out of the three language experience indices – (1) 'Language experience – features', (2) 'Language experience – phonemes', and (3) 'Language experience – phonological classes' – the model containing phoneme level information explained the most variance in the average thickness of the bilateral second TTG.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results.

claims.claim: The phoneme-level model outperformed the model containing the language experience index not accounting for any typological information.
claims.source: It also outperformed the model containing the language experience index not accounting for any typological information ('Language experience – no typology'), see Table 5.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results shown in Table 5.

claims.claim: The direction of the relationship between language experience weighted by typological distance was negative, with a small effect size (β = – 0.35, t = – 2.96, p=0.004, f2 = 0.07 and β = – 0.26, t = – 1.98, p=0.05, f2 = 0.04 for left and right hemisphere, respectively).
claims.source: The direction of the relationship between language experience weighted by typological distance was negative, and had a small effect size (β = – 0.35, t = – 2.96, p=0.004, f2 = 0.07 and β = – 0.26, t = – 1.98, p=0.05, f2 = 0.04 for left and right hemisphere, respectively), showing that the more extensive one's language experience, and the more varied at the phoneme level one's languages are, the thinner the second TTG cortex (see Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports statistical parameters and references Figure 2.

claims.claim: The more extensive one's language experience, and the more varied at the phoneme level one's languages are, the thinner the second TTG cortex.
claims.source: The direction of the relationship between language experience weighted by typological distance was negative, and had a small effect size (β = – 0.35, t = – 2.96, p=0.004, f2 = 0.07 and β = – 0.26, t = – 1.98, p=0.05, f2 = 0.04 for left and right hemisphere, respectively), showing that the more extensive one's language experience, and the more varied at the phoneme level one's languages are, the thinner the second TTG cortex (see Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The Results section interprets the statistical findings shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The index of multilingual language experience accounting for lexical distances between languages explained less variance than the index incorporating phoneme-level distances between languages, both in the left and the right hemisphere (R2Adj = 0.164 and R2Adj = 0.116 for left and right, respectively).
claims.source: We then entered this language experience measure accounting for lexical distances between the languages into linear models predicting the thickness of the second left and right TTG (controlling for participants' age, sex, and mean hemispheric thickness) and observed that the index of multilingual language experience accounting for lexical distances between languages explained less variance than the index incorporating phoneme-level distances between languages, both in the left and the right hemisphere (R2Adj = 0.164 and R2Adj = 0.116 for left and right, respectively).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports model comparison with lexical distance measure.

claims.claim: In the left hemisphere, the cumulative phoneme inventory measure explained variance in the thickness of the second TTG above and beyond language experience (β = – 0.004, t = – 2.910, p=0.004), with a small effect size (f2 = 0.06).
claims.source: In the left hemisphere, this measure explained variance in the thickness of the second TTG above and beyond language experience (β = – 0.004, t = – 2.910, p=0.004), with a small effect size (f2 = 0.06).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports statistical findings for the cumulative phoneme inventory analysis.

claims.claim: In the right hemisphere, the thickness of the second TTG was not significantly related to the 'cumulative phoneme inventory' measure (p=0.76), when also accounting for overall language experience irrespective of typology.
claims.source: In the right hemisphere, the thickness of the second TTG was not significantly related to the 'cumulative phoneme inventory' measure (p=0.76), when also accounting for overall language experience irrespective of typology.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports non-significant findings for the right hemisphere.

claims.claim: The thickness of the left second TTG in these participants was related to the specific characteristics of languages at the phoneme level of their phonological inventories, irrespective of when these languages were acquired.
claims.source: This result shows that the thickness of the left second TTG in these participants was related to the specific characteristics of languages at the phoneme level of their phonological inventories, irrespective of when these languages were acquired, while the thickness of the right second TTG was relatively more related to when and how many languages were learned (even though the typological distance information did improve the model fit, see Table 5), see Appendix 1—figure 6 and Appendix 1—table 4, and Appendix 1 – (Second TTG and effects of language typology).
claims.evidence: The Results section interprets the cumulative phoneme inventory findings.

claims.claim: 40 participants out of 136 (29.4%) had a single TTG (HG) in the right hemisphere.
claims.source: Yet, 40 participants out of 136 (29.4%) had a single TTG (HG) in the right hemisphere (versus only 6 participants, i.e., 4.4% in the left; see Table 4).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports descriptive statistics shown in Table 4.

claims.claim: In participants without posterior TTGs in the right hemisphere, the thickness of the first TTG was related to their language experience.
claims.source: The analysis revealed that in participants without posterior TTGs in the right hemisphere, the thickness of the first TTG was indeed related to their language experience.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports findings from the single TTG sub-group analysis.

claims.claim: The language experience index accounting for most variance in the thickness of the first TTG was the index not accounting for typological relations between multilinguals' languages.
claims.source: First, the language experience index accounting for most variance in the thickness of the first TTG was the index not accounting for typological relations between multilinguals' languages ('Language experience – no typology'), see Appendix 1—table 5.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results for the single TTG analysis.

claims.claim: The more extensive one's language experience, the thicker the HG (β=0.15, t=2.89, p=0.007; medium effect size: f2=0.237).
claims.source: Second, the direction of this effect was inverse to that found for participants with multiple TTGs: the more extensive one's language experience, the thicker the HG (β=0.15, t=2.89, p=0.007; medium effect size: f2=0.237), see Figure 3.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports statistical findings shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: No significant relationship was found between the thickness of the PT and language experience in the sub-group of participants with a single TTG (β=0.02, t=2.43, p=0.81).
claims.source: Of note, we did not find any significant relationship between the thickness of the PT and language experience in this sub-group of participants (β=0.02, t=2.43, p=0.81).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports non-significant findings for PT in single TTG participants.

claims.claim: For PT thickness, compared to a model including only covariates of no-interest, the model including the language experience index offered moderate evidence against it (BF10 = 0.16).
claims.source: In addition, for PT thickness, compared to a model including only covariates of no-interest, the model including the language experience index offered moderate evidence against it (BF10 = 0.16), suggesting that the observed effects between cortical thickness and language experience in the superior temporal plane are specific to gyri only, see Appendix 1—table 5 and Appendix 1 – (Language experience in participants with a single TTG).
claims.evidence: The Results section reports Bayesian model comparison results.

claims.claim: The observed effects between cortical thickness and language experience in the superior temporal plane are specific to gyri only.
claims.source: In addition, for PT thickness, compared to a model including only covariates of no-interest, the model including the language experience index offered moderate evidence against it (BF10 = 0.16), suggesting that the observed effects between cortical thickness and language experience in the superior temporal plane are specific to gyri only, see Appendix 1—table 5 and Appendix 1 – (Language experience in participants with a single TTG).
claims.evidence: The Results section interprets the Bayesian model comparison results.

claims.claim: Language experience ('Language experience – no typology') did significantly predict the average thickness of the second TTG in the right hemisphere in the replication sample (β = – 0.13, t = – 2.05, p=0.046; small effect size: f2 = 0.087).
claims.source: We again observed that language experience ('Language experience – no typology') did significantly predict the average thickness of the second TTG, but only in the right hemisphere (β = – 0.13, t = – 2.05, p=0.046; small effect size: f2 = 0.087), see Table 6.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports replication findings shown in Table 6.

claims.claim: In the replication sample, the language experience index weighted by phonological information at the phoneme level showed a better fit than the model without typological information, explaining 3% of additional variance in the average thickness of the right second TTG.
claims.source: Furthermore, similarly to the analysis on the main sample (see section 'Second TTG and effects of language typology'), the language experience index weighted by phonological information at the phoneme level ('Language experience – phonemes') showed a better fit than the model without typological information, explaining 3% of additional variance in the average thickness of the right second TTG.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results in the replication sample.

claims.claim: In the replication sample, the model including phonological feature-level information had a better fit to the thickness data and explained an additional 14% of the variance (11% more variance than the model with language experience weighted by phoneme-level distances).
claims.source: In contrast to the results of the main sample, however, this time the model including phonological feature-level information ('Language experience – features') had a better fit to the thickness data and explained an additional 14% of the variance (11% more variance than the model with language experience weighted by phoneme-level distances), see Table 6 and Figure 4C.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports model comparison results shown in Table 6 and Figure 4C.

claims.claim: No language experience indices were significantly related to the average thickness values of second TTG in the left hemisphere in the replication sample (β = – 0.03, t = – 0.53, p=0.60, and β = – 0.09, t = – 0.58, p=0.57, for language experience index without and with typological phoneme-level information, respectively).
claims.source: No language experience indices were significantly related to the average thickness values of second TTG in the left hemisphere (β = – 0.03, t = – 0.53, p=0.60, and β = – 0.09, t = – 0.58, p=0.57, for language experience index without and with typological phoneme-level information, respectively), see Figure 4 and Table 6.
claims.evidence: The Results section reports non-significant findings shown in Figure 4 and Table 6.

claims.claim: Multilingual language experience, quantified in a continuous manner, is related to the structure of the auditory cortex.
claims.source: Multilingual language experience, quantified in a continuous manner, is related to the structure of the auditory cortex.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the main finding of the study.

claims.claim: Multilingual language experience, weighed by the age of acquisition of the respective languages, is specifically related to the thickness of gyri (TTG) of the superior temporal plane.
claims.source: Using two independent samples of participants, we find replicable effects showing that multilingual language experience, weighed by the age of acquisition of the respective languages, is specifically related to the thickness of gyri (TTG) of the superior temporal plane.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes findings from both samples.

claims.claim: Typological distances between multilinguals' languages, in particular typological distance measures based on phonemes of the different languages (and to some degree on their acoustic and articulatory features), explains variation in TTG thickness above and beyond the effect of AoA alone.
claims.source: Moreover, we show that the typological distances between multilinguals' languages, in particular typological distance measures based on phonemes of the different languages (and to some degree on their acoustic and articulatory features), explains variation in TTG thickness above and beyond the effect of AoA alone.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the typology findings.

claims.claim: The effects are specific to the second TTG in people having at least one full posterior duplication, and to the first TTG in people having only one gyrus.
claims.source: The effects we find are specific to the second TTG in people having at least one full posterior duplication, and to the first TTG in people having only one gyrus.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the anatomical specificity of the findings.

claims.claim: HG is the first cortical relay station for auditory input.
claims.source: The anterior-most TTG, i.e., HG, is the first cortical relay station for auditory input.
claims.evidence: The Discussion states established knowledge about HG function.

claims.claim: HG and the TTG as a whole exhibit large individual variation in shape and size.
claims.source: HG and the TTG as a whole exhibit large individual variation in shape and size: some individuals have a single TTG, but duplications (complete or partial) and multiplications of the gyrus are also common, and have been observed both ex vivo (Geschwind and Levitsky, 1968) and in vivo (Marie et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies documenting anatomical variability.

claims.claim: The TTG are known to be formed before birth, in utero.
claims.source: The TTG are known to be formed before birth, in utero (Chi et al., 1977).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a study on prenatal TTG development.

claims.claim: Genes known to be involved in speech processing, in the development of the nervous system, and in X-linked deafness, have been related to the surface area and thickness of the left and right HG.
claims.source: Further, genes known to be involved in speech processing, in the development of the nervous system, and in X-linked deafness, have been related to the surface area and thickness of the left and right HG (Cai et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a genetic study on HG anatomy.

claims.claim: Relationships have been shown between both HG volume and TTG shape (i.e. duplication patterns) and auditory and language abilities that are thought to be relatively stable and thus possibly arising from predisposition.
claims.source: A body of work has shown relationships between both HG volume and TTG shape (i.e. duplication patterns) and auditory and language abilities that are thought to be relatively stable and thus possibly arising from predisposition, such as speech sound processing and learning abilities (Golestani et al., 2011; Golestani et al., 2007), linguistic tone learning (Wong et al., 2008), and general language aptitude (Turker et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites multiple studies linking TTG anatomy to language abilities.

claims.claim: Studies have shown larger HG and more TTG duplications in professional musicians.
claims.source: Studies have also shown larger HG and more TTG duplications in professional musicians (Schneider et al., 2005), and longitudinal work in children undergoing musical training shows that the gray matter volume of this region is relatively stable over the course of a year (Seither-Preisler et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies on musicians and HG anatomy.

claims.claim: Longitudinal work in children undergoing musical training shows that the gray matter volume of HG is relatively stable over the course of a year.
claims.source: Studies have also shown larger HG and more TTG duplications in professional musicians (Schneider et al., 2005), and longitudinal work in children undergoing musical training shows that the gray matter volume of this region is relatively stable over the course of a year (Seither-Preisler et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a longitudinal study on HG stability.

claims.claim: The bilinguals in the Ressel et al. study were not self-selected, so unlikely to have learned a second language because of a special talent for languages.
claims.source: Importantly, the bilinguals in their study were not self-selected, so unlikely to have learned a second language because of a special talent for languages.
claims.evidence: The Discussion describes characteristics of the Ressel et al. study sample.

claims.claim: The findings of the Ressel et al. study suggested that the HG volume differences arose from experience with a different phonological system, since Spanish and Catalan are quite similar at the lexical level but have different phonologies.
claims.source: The findings of the Ressel et al. study thus suggested that the HG volume differences arose from experience with a different phonological system, since Spanish and Catalan are quite similar at the lexical level but have different phonologies.
claims.evidence: The Discussion interprets the Ressel et al. findings in light of language typology.

claims.claim: Experience with multiple languages is associated with differences in the thickness of the TTG.
claims.source: More generally, our results show that experience with multiple languages is associated with differences in the thickness of the TTG, and that increasing degrees of multilingualism are linearly related to the structure of the TTG.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's main findings.

claims.claim: Increasing degrees of multilingualism are linearly related to the structure of the TTG.
claims.source: More generally, our results show that experience with multiple languages is associated with differences in the thickness of the TTG, and that increasing degrees of multilingualism are linearly related to the structure of the TTG.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's main findings.

claims.claim: Establishing that non-pathological environmental experiences are related to the morphology of TTG offers important insights into the adaptability of this early sensory region.
claims.source: Establishing that non-pathological environmental experiences are related to the morphology of TTG offers important insights into the adaptability of this early sensory region, and has important implications for our understanding of the neural underpinnings of auditory processing in general, which we outline below.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the study's implications.

claims.claim: The result aligns with recent findings of cortical surface area being relatively more associated with genetic factors and of cortical thickness being relatively more associated with environmental factors.
claims.source: The result aligns with recent findings of cortical surface area being relatively more associated with genetic factors and of cortical thickness being relatively more associated with environmental factors (e.g. Eyler et al., 2012; Grasby et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies supporting the interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Individual differences in the shape (i.e. duplication patterns) of the TTG seem to be related to how multilingualism will be accommodated by the thickness of the auditory brain regions.
claims.source: Individual differences in the shape (i.e. duplication patterns) of the TTG seem to, however, be related to how multilingualism will be accommodated by the thickness of the auditory brain regions: increasing thickness of the first gyrus when no duplications are present, and decreasing thickness of the second gyrus for participants with more than one TTG.
claims.evidence: The Discussion interprets the differential effects based on TTG anatomy.

claims.claim: Accounting for typology (i.e. including information regarding how languages spoken by the participants differed from each other in terms of their phonological systems) explained more variance in the cortical thickness data of the second TTG than an index of language experience accounting for the age of exposure to different languages alone.
claims.source: However, we observed that accounting for typology (i.e. including information regarding how languages spoken by the participants differed from each other in terms of their phonological systems) explained more variance in the cortical thickness data of the second TTG than an index of language experience accounting for the age of exposure to different languages alone.
claims.evidence: The Discussion emphasizes the importance of typological information in the findings.

claims.claim: Research has established relationships between population-level genetic factors (distribution of DCDC2 READ1 regulatory element) and characteristics of phoneme inventory of language(s) predominant in that population.
claims.source: It also has to be noted, however, that research has established relationships between population-level genetic factors (distribution of DCDC2 READ1 regulatory element) and characteristics of phoneme inventory of language(s) predominant in that population (DeMille et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2020), and that genetic influences on auditory cortex anatomy have previously been observed (Cai et al., 2014; Guadalupe et al., 2014), making it possible that our results may in some part also be related to genetic rather than purely environmental factors.
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies on genetic influences on language and brain anatomy.

claims.claim: Language experience is particularly related to gyri in the superior temporal plane, and not to the rest of the PT, nor to other auditory regions such as posterior STG.
claims.source: Our data show that, within the auditory cortex, language experience is particularly related to gyri in the superior temporal plane, and not to the rest of the PT (as shown in the analysis investigating the sub-sample of participants with a single gyrus in the right hemisphere), nor to other auditory regions such as posterior STG, as shown in the first, exploratory analysis across broader auditory cortex subregions.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the anatomical specificity of the findings.

claims.claim: Tuning to the different acoustic-phonetic features might be an experience-independent feature of the posterior STG.
claims.source: Tuning to the different acoustic-phonetic features might be an experience-independent feature of the posterior STG (i.e. it might be sensitive to features both present and absent from the languages a person knows), and therefore multilingualism might not induce any neuroplastic changes to this region.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for the lack of STG findings.

claims.claim: The findings may suggest that current language models might underestimate the role of early auditory regions (i.e. of HG and second TTG, when present) in phonological processing.
claims.source: Alternatively, our findings may suggest that current language models might underestimate the role of early auditory regions (i.e. of HG and second TTG, when present) in phonological processing, and support their role beyond an initial spectro-temporal analysis of speech sounds.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides an alternative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Fisher et al., 2018, has shown that speech sounds, and specifically vowel formants, are encoded in tonotopic auditory regions including HG and the STG.
claims.source: Functional neuroimaging work by Fisher et al., 2018, has shown that speech sounds, and specifically vowel formants, are encoded in tonotopic auditory regions including HG and the STG, suggesting that even early auditory regions such as HG and second TTG (when present) are involved in speech sound processing.
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a functional neuroimaging study.

claims.claim: Bonte et al., 2014 found that vowels can be decoded from fMRI signal of (among others) the temporal plane, HG, and sulcus.
claims.source: Similarly, Bonte et al., 2014 found that vowels can be decoded from fMRI signal of (among others) the temporal plane, HG, and sulcus (see also Jäncke et al., 2002; Obleser and Eisner, 2009; van Atteveldt et al., 2004 for findings of processing of isolated phonemes in the HG and PT regions);
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites multiple studies on phoneme processing in early auditory regions.

claims.claim: Rutten et al., 2019, showed that attending to speech sounds (stop consonants) in pseudowords results in an increase in the neural processing of higher temporal modulations in regions as early as HG and also in the PT.
claims.source: Rutten et al., 2019, showed that attending to speech sounds (stop consonants) in pseudowords results in an increase in the neural processing of higher temporal modulations in regions as early as HG and also in the PT.
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a study on speech sound processing in HG and PT.

claims.claim: The finding of an association between greater multilingual language experience and decreased thickness of the second TTG may arise from increased processing demands (and associated cortical pruning) inherent to the acquisition and mastery of many non-overlapping phonological inventories.
claims.source: It is therefore plausible that our finding of an association between greater multilingual language experience and decreased thickness of the second TTG arises from increased processing demands (and associated cortical pruning, see below) inherent to the acquisition and mastery of many non-overlapping phonological inventories.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Previous studies did not account for fine variation in the exact individual anatomy of the TTG (i.e. single versus multiplicated gyri).
claims.source: Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, previous studies did not account for fine variation in the exact individual anatomy of the TTG (i.e. single versus multiplicated gyri).
claims.evidence: The Discussion notes a methodological limitation of previous research.

claims.claim: Based on the current results, the second TTG (when present) could be a possible candidate for preferential phoneme processing.
claims.source: Our results may thus call for a re-evaluation of the specific anatomical site within the superior temporal plane in which phonemes are preferentially processed: based on our results, the second TTG (when present) could be a possible candidate.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes a new hypothesis based on the findings.

claims.claim: The replication sample included 31 individuals (i.e. 46% of participants) who spoke German and English, a language combination that has a phonological feature distance of zero.
claims.source: Specifically, the replication sample included 31 individuals (i.e. 46% of participants) who spoke German and English, a language combination that has a phonological feature distance of zero.
claims.evidence: The Discussion describes characteristics of the replication sample that may explain inconsistencies.

claims.claim: In the replication sample, the phonemes-based typological distance measure numerically explained more variance in the thickness of the second TTG than a composite language experience measure based on AoA of different languages.
claims.source: Notably, however, in the replication sample, the phonemes-based typological distance measure numerically explained more variance in the thickness of the second TTG than a composite language experience measure based on AoA of different languages, as observed in the main sample.
claims.evidence: The Discussion notes consistency in the pattern of results despite statistical differences.

claims.claim: The decreased thickness of the second TTG in relation to greater multilingualism may arise from functional remapping, experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency, or learning-related increased myelination.
claims.source: The decreased thickness of the second TTG in relation to greater multilingualism may arise from different, non-exclusive microstructural and physiological mechanisms, including functional remapping, experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency, or learning-related increased myelination.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes multiple potential mechanisms underlying the findings.

claims.claim: Primary auditory cortex is known to lie within the anterior-medial part of HG (i.e. the first TTG).
claims.source: Primary auditory cortex is known to lie within the anterior-medial part of HG (i.e. the first TTG; Rademacher et al., 1993), although there is no exact correspondence between cytoarchitectural and macrostructural boundaries (Rademacher et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies on the location of primary auditory cortex.

claims.claim: In vivo markers for human primary auditory cortex include tonotopy, increased myelination, and decreased cortical thickness.
claims.source: In vivo markers for human primary auditory cortex have been identified, including tonotopy, increased myelination (Dick et al., 2017), and decreased cortical thickness (Zoellner et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies identifying markers of primary auditory cortex.

claims.claim: There is evidence that in professional musicians, functional activation extends to posterior TTGs during listening to musical sounds, while activation is confined to HG in non-musicians.
claims.source: Also, there is evidence that in professional musicians, functional activation extends to posterior TTGs during listening to musical sounds, while activation is confined to HG in non-musicians (Schneider et al., unpublished findings).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites unpublished findings on musicians' auditory processing.

claims.claim: Experience-induced pruning is essential for maintaining an efficient and adaptive neural network.
claims.source: Experience-induced pruning is essential for maintaining an efficient and adaptive neural network. It reinforces relevant neural circuits for faster more efficient information processing, while diminishing those that are less active, or less beneficial.
claims.evidence: The Discussion explains the concept of neural pruning based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Phonologically more diverse language experience requires that the mapping of acoustic signal to sound categories is denser, more detailed, and more intricate.
claims.source: The cortical specialization may need to arise because phonologically more diverse language experience requires that the mapping of acoustic signal to sound categories is denser, more detailed, and more intricate.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a theoretical explanation for the findings.

claims.claim: Increased cognitive demand for speech perception may lead to neural plasticity, resulting in cortical specialization.
claims.source: As a result, the brain may need to engage in more intensive processing to discriminate between and accurately perceive the sound categories of each language. This increased cognitive demand may, in turn, require the auditory and language processing regions of the brain to adapt and become more efficient. Over time, this heightened effort for successful speech perception and sound discrimination may lead to neural plasticity, resulting in cortical specialization.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a theoretical explanation for the findings.

claims.claim: Gyri are more likely to host specialized functions due to their greater neuronal density or to specific micro-anatomical features and connectivity properties.
claims.source: Why this occurs in the second TTG and not in non-gyral portions of the superior temporal plane (i.e. in the PT more generally) remains to be explored in future work, but one possibility is that gyri are more likely to host such a specialized function due to their greater neuronal density or to specific micro-anatomical features and connectivity properties (i.e. greater proximity and thus more direct, local functional, and structural connectivity of neurons within the gyrus, as opposed to with neurons within the sulcal parts).
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for the gyrus-specific findings.

claims.claim: The neural efficiency account would be in line with the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism, according to which the 'peak efficiency' stage of multilingual functioning comes hand in hand with reductions in local volume.
claims.source: Either way, the neural efficiency account would be in line with the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism (Pliatsikas, 2020), according to which the 'peak efficiency' stage of multilingual functioning comes hand in hand with reductions in local volume.
claims.evidence: The Discussion relates the findings to an existing theoretical model.

claims.claim: The supplementary analysis investigating second TTG thickness in relation to proficient versus non-proficient languages points to the tentative conclusion that the observed reduced thickness results might be driven by experience with proficiently spoken languages.
claims.source: Of note, our supplementary analysis (see Appendix 1 – Effects of language proficiency) investigating second TTG thickness in relation to proficient versus non-proficient languages points to the tentative conclusion that the observed reduced thickness results might be driven by experience with proficiently spoken languages (more so than with non-proficiently spoken ones), aligning with the predictions of the Dynamic Restructuring Model.
claims.evidence: The Discussion references supplementary analyses supporting the interpretation.

claims.claim: Another potential microstructural mechanism underlying the thinner cortex result could be increased myelination of second TTG.
claims.source: Another potential microstructural mechanism underlying the thinner cortex result could be increased myelination of second TTG; this would again be in line with the idea that multilingual language experience leads to modifications such that the second TTG becomes more 'primary-like', since HG is characterized by higher myelination.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes an alternative mechanism based on known properties of HG.

claims.claim: It has been suggested that the apparent thinning of the ventral temporal cortex during childhood is actually driven by increased myelination.
claims.source: It has been suggested that the apparent thinning of the ventral temporal cortex during childhood (as argued by, e.g., Sowell et al., 2004) is actually driven by increased myelination, since increased myelination in deep cortical layers can shift the apparent gray-white boundary in MR images Natu et al., 2019; see also Mediavilla et al., 2022, for evidence on learning-related contraction of gray matter being associated with adaptive myelination in rodents.
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies on myelination and cortical thickness.

claims.claim: There might be different mechanisms underlying plasticity in regions more likely to contain primary versus secondary auditory cortex.
claims.source: We speculate that there might be different mechanisms underlying plasticity in regions more likely to contain primary versus secondary auditory cortex.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for the opposite direction of effects.

claims.claim: It may be more likely that experience-induced pruning occurs in secondary compared to primary regions, and that in primary regions, greater efficiency comes at the cost of a neuronal 'bulking'.
claims.source: In other words, it may be more likely that experience-induced pruning occurs in secondary compared to primary regions, and that in primary regions, greater efficiency comes at the cost of a neuronal 'bulking'.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for differential plasticity mechanisms.

claims.claim: In people who do not have a second TTG, HG needs to accommodate both lower-level auditory processing and also the processing of more complex speech sounds.
claims.source: Alternately but non-exclusively, it could be that in people who do not have a second TTG, HG needs to accommodate both lower-level auditory processing and also the processing of more complex speech sounds.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides an alternative speculative explanation.

claims.claim: TASH provides a 'best-of-both-worlds' approach, by being anatomically precise while involving little manual involvement with the data.
claims.source: Coupled with visual inspection of the data, TASH provides a 'best-of-both-worlds' approach, by being anatomically precise while involving little manual involvement with the data (which also tends to be error-prone).
claims.evidence: The Discussion describes the advantages of the TASH method.

claims.claim: TASH identifies more multiplications of the TTG than previously reported.
claims.source: The measures we obtained align with the high degree of variability reported in previous literature, but they also seem to be more sensitive, since we identify more multiplications of the TTG than previously reported.
claims.evidence: The Discussion compares TASH results to previous literature.

claims.claim: In Marie et al., 2015, out of 232 subjects, 204 (88%) had one gyrus (including partially duplicated) in the left hemisphere, 28 (12%) had a complete posterior duplication.
claims.source: For example, in Marie et al., 2015, out of 232 subjects, 204 (88%) had one gyrus (including partially duplicated) in the left hemisphere, 28 (12%) had a complete posterior duplication; the prevalence of further multiplications was not assessed in that study.
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a previous study for comparison.

claims.claim: In the current data, a minority of participants (4%) presented only one gyrus in the left hemisphere, and most of them had either two (57%) or three (35%) separate gyri.
claims.source: In our data, a minority of participants (4%) presented only one gyrus in the left hemisphere, and most of them had either two (57%) or three (35%) separate gyri.
claims.evidence: The Discussion reports descriptive statistics from the current study.

claims.claim: TASH identifies gyri based on anatomical landmarks and curvature values, and is surface-based rather than volume-based.
claims.source: TASH identifies gyri based on anatomical landmarks and curvature values, and unlike previous descriptive work is surface-based rather than volume-based.
claims.evidence: The Discussion describes the TASH methodology.

claims.source: It therefore might be more sensitive to shallow cortical folds that might otherwise not be discernable in volume-based manual labeling.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a speculative explanation for TASH's sensitivity.

claims.claim: Variability in shape of the auditory regions is absent from other, evolutionarily older, species: macaques' auditory cortex is flat, and some chimpanzees have only a single gyrus.
claims.source: Notably, such variability in shape of the auditory regions is absent from other, evolutionarily older, species: macaques' auditory cortex is flat, and some chimpanzees have only a single gyrus (Hackett et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a comparative anatomy study.

claims.claim: By showing that a human-specific experience, i.e., speaking multiple languages, is reflected in the anatomy of cortical regions that seem to be evolutionarily particular to humans, the study contributes to informing both models of neuroplasticity and of language evolution.
claims.source: By showing that a human-specific experience, i.e., speaking multiple languages, is reflected in the anatomy of cortical regions that seem to be evolutionarily particular to humans, we contribute to informing both models of neuroplasticity and of language evolution.
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides a broader interpretation of the study's significance.

claims.claim: The findings support the idea that experience with typologically similar languages might be different from experience with typologically distant languages.
claims.source: Apart from showing that individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations, our findings also support the idea that experience with typologically similar languages might be different from experience with typologically distant languages (Antoniou, 2019; Berthele, 2020; Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Discussion relates the findings to existing theoretical ideas with citations.

claims.claim: Individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations.
claims.source: Apart from showing that individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations, our findings also support the idea that experience with typologically similar languages might be different from experience with typologically distant languages (Antoniou, 2019; Berthele, 2020; Li et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Discussion provides an interpretation of the findings.

results.result: The study analyzed data from 204 participants across two independent samples (main sample: 136 participants; replication sample: 68 participants) who were exposed to 1-7 languages representing 36 different languages total.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C29, C30, C38, C39, and C40 provide consistent and detailed sample characteristics including participant numbers, language exposure range, and linguistic diversity. The data are explicitly reported in both abstract and methods sections with specific demographic details.

results.result: There is a negative relationship between the thickness of the second transverse temporal gyrus (TTG) bilaterally and participants' degree of multilingualism, with small effect sizes (left: β = -0.35, p=0.004, f²=0.07; right: β = -0.26, p=0.05, f²=0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C52, C57, and C58 consistently report the main finding with specific statistical parameters. The negative relationship is demonstrated with appropriate statistical tests, effect sizes, and significance levels. Figure 2 provides visual confirmation of this relationship.

results.result: Models incorporating phoneme-level typological information in the language experience index explained the most variance in TTG thickness compared to models without typological information or with other typological measures (features or phonological classes).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C55, C56, and C76 report model comparison results showing that phoneme-level information provides the best model fit. Table 5 presents detailed model comparison statistics including R² values and Bayes factors supporting this conclusion.

results.result: More extensive and phonologically diverse language experience is associated with thinner cortices in the second TTG, with the left hemisphere showing sensitivity to phoneme inventory characteristics irrespective of age of acquisition.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C58, and C62 provide converging evidence for the interpretation of the negative relationship. The cumulative phoneme inventory analysis (C60) provides additional support showing that phoneme-level characteristics explain variance beyond age of acquisition effects in the left hemisphere.

results.result: The negative relationship between TTG thickness and multilingualism was partially replicated in an independent sample, with significant effects in the right hemisphere (p=0.046) but not the left hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C70, C71, C72, and C73 show partial replication. While the right hemisphere showed significant effects and the phoneme-level model showed better fit, the left hemisphere results were non-significant (p=0.60). The replication is incomplete, and the authors note sample composition differences (C103) that may explain inconsistencies.

results.result: The findings support the interpretation of experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency, where phonologically diverse language experience leads to cortical specialization through synaptic pruning in the second TTG.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C100, C105, C109, C110, and C111 present theoretical interpretations of the findings. While the negative relationship is well-established, the specific microstructural mechanisms (pruning vs. myelination) remain speculative. The cross-sectional design precludes direct evidence for these mechanisms, and alternative explanations (C115, C116) are also proposed.

results.result: Experience with typologically distant languages impacts the brain differently than experience with similar languages, as evidenced by the superior explanatory power of phoneme-level distance measures.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C128 are supported by the model comparison results (C55, C56) showing that typological distance measures explain additional variance beyond simple language experience. The lexical distance comparison (C59) further strengthens this conclusion by showing phonological measures outperform lexical measures.

results.result: Early auditory regions (second TTG when present) appear to represent phoneme-level cross-linguistic information, contrary to established models suggesting phonological processing occurs in more lateral posterior STG and STS.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C96, and C102 present a novel interpretation challenging established models. While the structural findings in TTG are well-supported, the functional interpretation is speculative. The lack of effects in posterior STG (C94) is noted, but alternative explanations (C95) are also provided. Functional neuroimaging evidence is cited (C97, C98, C99) but the structural-functional link remains inferential.

results.result: In participants with a single TTG in the right hemisphere (29.4% of sample), language experience showed a positive relationship with HG thickness (β=0.15, p=0.007, f²=0.237) but no relationship with PT thickness, with effects specific to gyri.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 report findings from the single TTG subgroup analysis with appropriate statistics. The opposite direction of effect compared to the second TTG is clearly documented, and Bayesian analysis (C68) provides evidence that effects are specific to gyri. However, the sample size is relatively small (n=40) and replication was not performed.

results.result: In an exploratory analysis of broader auditory regions, only the average thickness of the planum temporale (PT) bilaterally was related to language experience (p=0.01), with more extensive language experience associated with thinner PT.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C49 report the initial exploratory finding that motivated the more detailed TTG analysis. The statistical significance is clearly stated, though this finding was later refined to show specificity to gyri rather than PT as a whole (C69, C94).

results.result: TTG showed high individual variability in duplication patterns (mean: 2.375 gyri in left hemisphere, 1.84 in right hemisphere), but the number of gyri was not related to language experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C51, and C63 report descriptive statistics on TTG anatomy with appropriate statistical tests showing no relationship between number of gyri and language experience. Table 4 provides detailed breakdown of duplication patterns across the sample.

results.result: Vertex-wise analysis identified a cluster in the left superior temporal plane corresponding to the second TTG location that was negatively related to language experience (p<0.0001, uncorrected), with no significant clusters in the right hemisphere at the same threshold.
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C54 report vertex-wise analysis results that corroborate the ROI-based findings. However, the results are uncorrected for multiple comparisons, which is a significant limitation. The explanation for lack of right hemisphere findings (greater anatomical variability, C54) is plausible but the statistical threshold issue remains.

results.result: Lexical distance measures explained less variance than phoneme-level measures, and cumulative phoneme inventory explained additional variance in left second TTG thickness (β=-0.004, p=0.004, f²=0.06) but not in the right hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, and C61 report additional analyses demonstrating the specificity of phonological (vs. lexical) effects and hemispheric differences. The statistics are clearly reported with appropriate effect sizes, supporting the interpretation that phonological characteristics specifically drive the observed effects.

results.result: The findings align with recent large-scale genetic studies showing that cortical surface area is relatively more influenced by genetics while cortical thickness reflects environmentally driven neuroplasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C23, and C90 cite appropriate large-scale genetic studies (Grasby et al., 2020) to contextualize the findings. The interpretation that thickness (but not surface area or number of gyri) relates to language experience is consistent with this framework.

results.result: Individual differences in TTG duplication patterns appear to modulate how multilingualism affects cortical thickness, with opposite directions of effect in participants with single versus multiple TTGs, possibly reflecting different plasticity mechanisms in primary versus secondary auditory regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C117, C118, and C119 present speculative interpretations of the opposite direction effects. While the empirical findings are well-documented, the mechanistic explanations remain hypothetical. The cross-sectional design and lack of functional data limit the ability to test these hypotheses.

results.result: The TASH segmentation method identified more TTG multiplications than previously reported in the literature, possibly due to its surface-based approach and sensitivity to shallow cortical folds.
results.evaluation: Claims C120, C121, C124, and C125 describe methodological advantages of TASH. The comparison with previous literature (C122, C123) shows clear differences in duplication prevalence (4% vs. 88% with single gyrus in left hemisphere), though the explanation for this difference (C125) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: Three typological distance measures were constructed based on PHOIBLE database: acoustic/articulatory features (37 binary features), phonemes (Jaccard distance), and phonological classes (167 classes), which showed low to moderate positive correlations with each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 describe the methodology for constructing typological distance measures with appropriate detail and citations. Table 2 shows the correlations between measures. The example calculations (C44, C45, C46) are correctly computed based on cited phoneme counts.

results.result: The anatomical organization of the auditory cortex includes primary auditory regions in the first TTG (Heschl's gyrus), with the planum polare anterior and planum temporale posterior to HG, and the superior temporal sulcus separating STG from middle temporal gyrus. TTG shows high individual variability in shape and size.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C15 present established anatomical knowledge with appropriate citations. These are well-documented facts in the neuroanatomy literature and provide necessary background for interpreting the study's findings.

results.result: HG is the first cortical relay station for auditory input, exhibits large individual variation, is formed prenatally, has genetic influences on its anatomy, and shows relationships with auditory/language abilities and musical training, with relatively stable gray matter volume over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 summarize established knowledge about HG with appropriate citations. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings, particularly regarding the balance between genetic predisposition and experience-dependent plasticity.

results.result: Research has established relationships between population-level genetic factors (DCDC2 READ1 regulatory element) and phoneme inventory characteristics, suggesting that genetic factors may partially contribute to the observed results.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 cites appropriate studies (DeMille et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2020) documenting genetic influences on phonological systems. This represents an important caveat to the environmental plasticity interpretation, though the authors acknowledge this limitation appropriately.

results.result: There is no consensus on functional parcellation of auditory cortex, with recent parallel processing models contrasting with hierarchical models. Posterior STG is considered crucial for phonological processing and encoding acoustic-articulatory features, while primary auditory regions including HG have been argued not to be necessary for speech perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 accurately summarize current debates in the auditory neuroscience literature with appropriate citations. These provide the theoretical framework motivating the study's predictions and interpretation.

results.result: Environmental effects on cortical thickness may be tied to microstructural changes including dendritic modifications, synaptogenesis/pruning, and glial growth. Increased thickness may reflect synaptogenesis and dendritic growth, while thinning may result from increased myelination or synaptic pruning.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 cite appropriate review papers and studies on neuroplasticity mechanisms. These provide the theoretical basis for interpreting cortical thickness changes, though the specific mechanisms in the current study remain speculative.

results.result: Ressel et al., 2012 found that lifelong bilingualism with Spanish and Catalan was associated with increased HG volume in non-self-selected bilinguals, suggesting the effect arose from phonological rather than lexical differences between the languages.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C85, and C86 accurately describe and interpret a key prior study. The interpretation regarding phonological vs. lexical effects is reasonable given that Spanish and Catalan are lexically similar but phonologically distinct.

results.result: Phonological perceptual space is shaped relatively early in life, motivating the use of age of acquisition (AoA) weighting in the language experience index, which was operationalized using Shannon's entropy with high values indicating more diverse experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C32 provide appropriate justification for the methodological approach with citation to developmental literature (Werker and Hensch, 2015). The entropy-based quantification is clearly explained and appropriate for the research question.

results.result: The study predicted that posterior STG thickness would relate to language experience and acoustic-articulatory features. According to current models, multilingualism could induce both increases (initial stages) and decreases (peak efficiency) in brain morphology, with positive relationships indicating expansion to accommodate variability and negative relationships suggesting specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 clearly state the study's predictions with appropriate citations to theoretical models (Pliatsikas, 2020). The bidirectional predictions are appropriately grounded in the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism.

results.result: Language experience was specifically related to gyri in the superior temporal plane, not to PT or posterior STG. The lack of STG effects might indicate experience-independent tuning to acoustic-phonetic features, or alternatively suggest that current models underestimate the role of early auditory regions in phonological processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C95, and C96 present the anatomical specificity of findings with two competing interpretations. While the empirical observation is well-supported, the functional interpretations remain speculative. The study design cannot definitively distinguish between these alternatives.

results.result: Functional neuroimaging studies have shown that speech sounds and vowel formants are encoded in early auditory regions including HG and the temporal plane, and that attending to speech sounds increases neural processing in these regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C98, and C99 cite appropriate functional neuroimaging studies supporting the involvement of early auditory regions in phonological processing. These citations provide important context for the structural findings, though they do not directly demonstrate the functional significance of the observed thickness differences.

results.result: The replication sample included 46% of participants speaking German and English (phonological feature distance of zero), which may explain inconsistencies with the main sample. However, the phoneme-based measure still numerically explained more variance than the AoA-only measure.
results.evaluation: Claims C103 and C104 provide a reasonable explanation for the partial replication, noting sample composition differences while also highlighting consistency in the pattern of results. This demonstrates appropriate consideration of factors affecting replication.

results.result: Primary auditory cortex lies within the anterior-medial part of HG, with in vivo markers including tonotopy, increased myelination, and decreased thickness. In musicians, functional activation extends to posterior TTGs during music listening, while non-musicians show activation confined to HG.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C107, and C108 cite appropriate studies on primary auditory cortex localization and function. The musician findings (C108) are from unpublished data, which is a limitation, but the other claims are well-supported by published literature.

results.result: The neural efficiency interpretation aligns with the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism, where peak efficiency is associated with volume reductions. Supplementary analyses suggest effects are driven by proficiently spoken languages.
results.evaluation: Claims C113 and C114 relate findings to theoretical models and reference supplementary analyses. While the theoretical alignment is appropriate, the proficiency analysis (C114) is described as "tentative" and is not presented in the main results, limiting confidence in this conclusion.

results.result: Increased myelination of the second TTG could be an alternative mechanism underlying cortical thinning, consistent with the idea that multilingual experience makes the second TTG more 'primary-like'. Studies suggest apparent cortical thinning during development may be driven by increased myelination.
results.evaluation: Claims C115 and C116 propose an alternative mechanism with appropriate citations. However, this remains speculative as the study did not measure myelination directly. The cited developmental studies provide plausibility but not direct evidence for this mechanism in the current context.

results.result: Variability in auditory region shape is absent in evolutionarily older species (macaques have flat auditory cortex, some chimpanzees have only single gyrus). The study contributes to understanding neuroplasticity and language evolution by showing human-specific language experience reflected in evolutionarily particular cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C127 cite appropriate comparative anatomy studies and provide a reasonable evolutionary interpretation of the findings. The connection between human-specific experience and human-specific anatomy is conceptually sound, though the evolutionary implications remain somewhat speculative.

results.result: Individual anatomy appears to constrain the architecture of phonological representations, as evidenced by the differential effects of multilingualism depending on TTG duplication patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 provides a reasonable interpretation of the findings showing opposite direction effects in participants with different TTG anatomy. The empirical basis (different effects in single vs. multiple TTG participants) is well-established, supporting this conclusion about anatomical constraints.

results.result: The study analyzed data from over 200 participants (136 in main sample, 68 in replication sample) exposed to 1–7 languages across 36 different languages total. The samples included monolinguals and multilinguals with diverse linguistic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge and praise the sample characteristics. Reviewer 1 states the project is 'notable for using a relatively large sample, and confirming the primary finding in a second sample.' Reviewer 2 notes 'A relatively large group of subjects with a range of linguistic backgrounds' as a strength. Reviewer 3 describes 'The primary sample is moderately large for a study that focuses on brain-behaviour relationships; a somewhat smaller replication sample is also deployed.'

results.result: There is a negative relationship between the thickness of the second transverse temporal gyrus (TTG) bilaterally and participants' degree of multilingualism. Models incorporating phoneme-level information explained the most variance in TTG thickness, showing that more extensive and phonologically diverse language experience is associated with thinner cortices in the second TTG.
results.evaluation: The editor states this provides 'convincing evidence that experience with multilingualism in general, and with larger phonological inventories specifically, is related to differences in the structure of the transverse temporal gyri.' Reviewer 2 notes 'solid evidence for there being a negative relationship between language experience and the right 2nd transverse temporal gyrus.' Reviewer 1 affirms 'the evidence suggests that learning more phonemes...leads to experience-related plasticity brain regions implicated in early auditory processing.'

results.result: Typological distances between multilinguals' languages, particularly phoneme-level information, explained variation in TTG thickness above and beyond age of acquisition alone. This suggests that phonologically diverse language experience is specifically associated with cortical thickness differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 highlights as a strength 'The use of entropy measures to quantify language experience and include typological distance measures' and notes 'some evidence for the relationship representing phoneme-level cross-linguistic information.' Reviewer 1 states 'the fine-grained relationships with phonological diversity seem less likely to emerge from aptitude rather than experience,' supporting the interpretation. The editor emphasizes this as part of the 'important findings.'

results.result: The pattern of negative relationship between TTG thickness and multilingualism was tested in a replication sample. The right hemisphere second TTG showed significant effects, though the left hemisphere did not replicate and feature-level information showed better fit than phoneme-level in the replication sample.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes a weakness: 'Only the association in the right hemisphere 2nd TTG is replicated but this is not reflected in the discussion or the conclusions.' Reviewer 3 states 'the results only partially replicated in that sample' due to smaller sample size and weaker statistical power. The editor acknowledges replication as notable but reviewers clearly identify the partial nature of replication as a limitation.

results.result: In participants with a single TTG in the right hemisphere (29.4% of sample), the thickness of the first TTG (Heschl's gyrus) showed a positive relationship with language experience, opposite to the pattern in participants with multiple TTGs. This effect was best explained by language experience without typological information and was specific to gyri, not planum temporale.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly critique this finding. Reviewer 3 notes the study 'benefit[s] from the careful use of brain segmentation techniques that nicely capture key landmarks and account for vagaries in the structure of STG that can vary across individuals (e.g., the number of transverse temporal gyri varies from 1-4 across individuals).' The anatomical specificity is implicitly accepted as part of the rigorous approach praised by reviewers.

results.result: The findings support the idea of experience-driven pruning and neural efficiency, suggesting that multilingual language experience is related to auditory cortex structure through mechanisms including synaptic pruning, increased myelination, or functional remapping. The pattern aligns with the Dynamic Restructuring Model of bilingualism.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states the findings 'strongly point to experience-dependent plasticity related to language experience as a driver of neuroanatomy of the auditory cortex.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the team has been careful in discussion of these findings' and that 'the fine-grained relationships with phonological diversity seem less likely to emerge from aptitude rather than experience,' supporting the plasticity interpretation over genetic predisposition.

results.result: Experience with typologically distant languages appears to impact the brain differently than experience with similar languages, suggesting that individual anatomy constrains the architecture of phonological representations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'The authors have satisfied my curiosity regarding other potential confounds in the data, including measurements of lexical distance as well as phonological typology.' This indicates reviewer acceptance of the typological distance findings. The editor's statement about 'larger phonological inventories specifically' being related to TTG structure implicitly supports this claim.

results.result: Early auditory regions (HG and second TTG) seem to represent phoneme-level cross-linguistic information, contrary to established models suggesting phonological processing happens in more lateral posterior STG and STS. The findings suggest current language models may underestimate the role of early auditory regions in phonological processing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this interpretation. Reviewer 3 states 'The results are first and foremost quite fascinating and I do think they make a compelling case for the different ways in which linguistic experience shapes auditory cortex.' The editor describes these as 'important findings,' implicitly accepting the challenge to established models.

results.result: In exploratory analyses, only the planum temporale (PT) thickness bilaterally was related to language experience at p=0.01, with more extensive language experience associated with thinner PT. However, focused analyses showed language experience is particularly related to gyri in the superior temporal plane, not to PT or posterior STG.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not critique these exploratory findings. Reviewer 2 notes as a strength 'The full analysis of the structure of the superior temporal cortex including cortical volume, area, as well as the shape of the transverse gyrus/gyri.' The comprehensive approach to examining different regions is praised, implicitly accepting the specificity of findings to TTG.

results.result: Participants showed high variability in TTG anatomy (average 2.375 gyri in left hemisphere, 1.84 in right), with 29.4% having a single TTG in the right hemisphere. The number of gyri was not related to language experience, but individual differences in TTG shape appear related to how multilingualism is accommodated by cortical thickness.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly praises 'the careful use of brain segmentation techniques that nicely capture key landmarks and account for vagaries in the structure of STG that can vary across individuals.' Reviewer 2 notes as a strength the study's exploration of 'the shape and number of the transverse gyri in relation to language proficiency.' The anatomical variability findings are accepted as part of the rigorous methodology.

results.result: Lexical distance measures explained less variance than phoneme-level measures. Cumulative phoneme inventory explained additional variance in left second TTG thickness beyond language experience, but not in the right hemisphere, suggesting hemispheric differences in how typological information is represented.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'The authors have satisfied my curiosity regarding other potential confounds in the data, including measurements of lexical distance as well as phonological typology,' indicating acceptance of these comparative analyses. No reviewer challenges the hemispheric differences reported.

results.result: Research has established relationships between population-level genetic factors (DCDC2 READ1 regulatory element) and phoneme inventory characteristics, and genetic influences on auditory cortex anatomy have been observed, making it possible that results may partly relate to genetic rather than purely environmental factors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'Discussion of potential genetic differences underlying the findings is interesting. It does represent one alternative account that does not have to do with plasticity/experience, as the authors acknowledge.' However, Reviewer 1 states 'the fine-grained relationships with phonological diversity seem less likely to emerge from aptitude rather than experience,' suggesting the genetic alternative is less plausible. The reviewers acknowledge but do not fully resolve this alternative explanation.

results.result: The replication sample included 46% of participants who spoke German and English (phonological feature distance of zero), which may explain why feature-level models performed differently. However, phoneme-based measures still numerically explained more variance than AoA-only measures.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes as a weakness 'The replication dataset differed in more ways than the more frequent combination of English and German experience, as mentioned in the discussion. Specifically, the fraction of monolinguals was higher in the replication dataset and the samples came from different scanners. It would be better if the primary and replication datasets were more equally matched.' This indicates concern about sample differences affecting interpretation.

results.result: The TASH segmentation method provides anatomically precise identification of TTG with minimal manual involvement and appears more sensitive than previous methods, identifying more multiplications of TTG (57% with two gyri, 35% with three in left hemisphere) than previously reported.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly praises 'the careful use of brain segmentation techniques that nicely capture key landmarks and account for vagaries in the structure of STG that can vary across individuals.' Reviewer 2 notes as a strength 'The full analysis of the structure of the superior temporal cortex including cortical volume, area, as well as the shape of the transverse gyrus/gyri.' The methodological approach is accepted without critique.

results.result: The study operationalized language experience using Shannon's entropy equation, with high entropy values indicating more diverse language experience. The three typological distance measures (features, phonemes, phonological classes) showed low to moderate positive correlations with each other.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly highlights as a strength 'The use of entropy measures to quantify language experience and include typological distance measures allows for a more general interpretation of the results and is an important step toward respecting and making use of linguistic diversity in neurolinguistic experiments.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors use a custom measure of multilingualism (accounting for both number of languages as well as age of acquisition) and three measures of phonological diversity' as part of the rigorous approach.
